title: Studying how children learn words
instructions: Match each finding with the researcher it belongs to.
text: How do young children learn so many words so quickly? In the 1970s, Susan Carey showed that children can pick up a rough meaning of a new word after hearing it only once, a process she called fast mapping. Later, Paul Bloom argued that this ability is not special to language, since children can also remember a fact about an object after a single exposure. Meanwhile, Anne Fernald studied the speech that parents use with babies, and found that its exaggerated pitch helps infants pay attention to the words that matter. More recently, Michael Tomasello has emphasised the social side of word learning: in his experiments, toddlers worked out which object an adult meant by following where the adult was looking, rather than simply linking a word to whatever they themselves were looking at.

items.s: Children use an adult's gaze to identify what a word refers to.
A single hearing of a word can be enough to start learning it.
Quick learning after one exposure is not limited to words.
The way parents speak to babies helps them focus on key words.

title: Three ancient cities
instructions: Match each statement with the city it describes.
text: Three of the earliest cities offer interesting contrasts. Uruk, in what is now Iraq, was home to perhaps forty thousand people by 3000 BCE, and its scribes developed one of the first writing systems, largely to keep records of grain and livestock. Mohenjo-daro, in the Indus Valley, is remarkable for its planning: streets were laid out in a grid, and most houses had access to a covered drainage system. Yet no large palaces or temples have been found there, which has led some to suggest it was governed without a single powerful ruler. Çatalhöyük, in Turkey, is older than both but hardly a city in the modern sense; its houses were packed so closely together that there were no streets at all, and residents entered their homes through holes in the roofs.

items.s: It may not have had one strong leader.
People climbed into their houses from above.
Writing was used to record farm products.
It had an organised system for waste water.
It is the oldest of the three.

title: Views on the four-day week
instructions: Match each opinion with the person who expressed it.
text: Opinions on the four-day working week vary widely. Economist Laura Chen argues that the benefits have been exaggerated, noting that most trials so far have taken place in office-based firms where output is hard to measure. Business owner Raj Patel, whose company adopted the shorter week two years ago, says that the biggest change has been in recruitment: he now receives far more applications for every job. Trade union official Maria Gómez supports the idea but warns that it must not become an excuse to squeeze five days of work into four longer days. Finally, psychologist Tom Erikson points to evidence that staff on shorter weeks report less stress, but he stresses that these reports come from the employees themselves and may be influenced by their wish for the policy to continue.

items.s: A shorter week makes it easier to attract job applicants.
Self-reported benefits may not be fully reliable.
Trials have mostly been in one kind of workplace.
Working hours per day should not simply increase.

title: Explaining bird migration
instructions: Match each idea with the scientist it is linked to.
text: Scientists have proposed several explanations for how migrating birds find their way. Gustav Kramer showed in the 1950s that caged starlings oriented themselves using the position of the sun, adjusting for the time of day. Stephen Emlen, working with young buntings in a planetarium, found that they learned to identify the point in the sky around which the stars rotate, and used it to find north. Wolfgang Wiltschko demonstrated that robins could sense the Earth's magnetic field, since their direction changed when the magnetic field around their cage was altered. Floriano Papi, studying homing pigeons, proposed that smell also plays a part, after finding that pigeons whose sense of smell was blocked had difficulty returning home from unfamiliar places.

items.s: Birds may use scent to navigate.
Birds can take account of the time when using the sun.
Changing a magnetic field altered birds' direction.
Young birds learn the centre of the stars' rotation.

title: Early photography
instructions: Match each achievement with the inventor.
text: Several people contributed to the invention of photography. Joseph Nicéphore Niépce produced the oldest surviving photograph in the 1820s, a view from his window that required an exposure lasting many hours. His partner, Louis Daguerre, later developed a process that produced sharp images on polished metal plates, with exposures of a few minutes, but each image was unique and could not be copied. In England, William Henry Fox Talbot invented a method that created a paper negative, from which any number of positive prints could be made. John Herschel, a scientist and friend of Talbot, found a chemical way to fix images so that they did not fade, and is also credited with popularising the word photography itself.

items.s: made images that could not be reproduced
made the oldest photograph that still exists
helped to make images permanent
allowed many copies to be printed from one image
is associated with the name of the new art
